trap.why: Credential stuffing tries each leaked username once or twice from many IPs, so per-account lockout barely triggers, while attackers can deliberately lock out real users.
trap.probe: Layered defences: risk-based throttling, breached-password checks, MFA, bot detection and monitoring.
trap.say: "Layered: rate limits per IP, network and device fingerprint, breached-password checks, risk-based step-up MFA, bot detection, and alerting on login success-rate anomalies, instead of hard per-account lockouts."

thesis: Credential stuffing uses leaked username and password pairs at scale, distributed across many IPs. Defend in layers: make guessing expensive and slow, detect automation, stop known-breached passwords, require stronger factors when risk is high, and watch for anomalies, without hard lockouts that attackers can weaponise.
pitch: Attackers take credentials leaked from other sites and try them, usually once per account, from botnets and residential proxies. Per-account lockout barely helps and lets attackers lock out real users. I'd layer defences. Rate limits by IP, subnet, ASN and device fingerprint, with progressive delays rather than hard blocks. Bot detection: challenges, device and behaviour signals, and blocking known abusive infrastructure. Breached-password checks at signup and login, for example against Have I Been Pwned's k-anonymity API, forcing resets for exposed passwords. MFA, ideally passkeys or app-based, and risk-based step-up for logins from new devices or locations. Generic error messages that don't reveal whether an account exists. And monitoring: a sudden drop in login success rate or spike in failures is the signature of an attack. After a likely takeover, notify users of new-device logins and make session revocation easy.

points.d: Leaked credential pairs, one or two tries per account, spread across many IPs to evade simple limits.
Limits by IP, network, device fingerprint and globally on the login endpoint, with progressive delays.
Device and behavioural signals, challenges for suspicious traffic, and reputation lists for abusive infrastructure.
Reject or force resets for passwords found in known breaches, using privacy-preserving lookups.
Strong second factors or passkeys make stolen passwords far less useful; step up based on risk.
Same response and timing for unknown users and wrong passwords.
Alert on login failure spikes and success-rate drops; notify users of new devices; easy session revocation.

decision: Layered, risk-based defences with soft throttling over hard lockouts; passkeys or MFA for high-value accounts; dedicated monitoring of the login funnel.
numbers: Typical stuffing success rates are low, often well under a few percent, but at millions of attempts that still means thousands of compromised accounts.
pitfalls: Hard lockouts that attackers use to deny service.
Rate limiting by IP only, defeated by proxies.
Error messages that confirm whether an email is registered.
No alerting on login anomalies, so attacks are found from customer complaints.

followups.q: How do you protect the password reset flow?
followups.a: Same rate limiting and bot defences, single-use time-limited tokens, notifying the user, and not revealing whether the account exists.

followups.q: Should SMS be the second factor?
followups.a: It's better than nothing but vulnerable to SIM swap; prefer app-based codes or passkeys, especially for financial accounts.

followups.q: How do you handle a confirmed takeover?
followups.a: Revoke sessions and tokens, force a password reset, review recent account changes (payout details, email), and reverse fraudulent actions.

example: A fintech saw login traffic triple overnight with a 0.4% success rate from 40,000 IPs. Device-fingerprint rate limits, a bot challenge for unrecognised devices, and forced resets for breached passwords cut attempts by 95%; new-device step-up MFA stopped the remaining takeovers.
